newsitem.title: USA: HarperCollins sets 420 layoffs, $270 million charge.
newsitem.headline: HarperCollins sets 420 layoffs, $270 million charge.

text.p: News Corp. said Monday it was cutting 420 jobs at its HarperCollins book publishing unit and would take a one-time charge of $270 million for restructuring the troubled U.S. operation.
But the huge media company controlled by Rupert Murdoch said it had no plans to sell HarperCollins after a year-long effort to restructure the book publisher.

New Corp. acknowledged it has received "expressions of interest" about its businesses, including HarperCollins, and issued a statement "as a result of unusual speculation in the media about the future of HarperCollins." Publishing industry officials have speculated that New Corp. would sell the unit.
The publisher said it "will focus its publishing efforts on a defined number of strategic areas" and a spokesman said it will scale back in non-commercial fiction.

"HarperCollins is a key asset and immensely important to our company (and) plays an important role in each of the primary geographic areas where the company conducts considerable business," Murdoch said in a statement.
Analysts said the layoffs and the charge were a step toward fixing a troubled operation.
"That's a fairly significant writedown," said Chris Dixon, an analyst at PaineWebber. "There are clearly a number of problems at HarperCollins."
A spokesman said the writeoff would be a mixture of cancelling and buying out author contracts as well as writing off inventories of unsold books.
News Corp. said about 220 jobs have already been cut and another 200 will still be slashed, including 40 in the United States.

Industry executives said HarperCollins has gone through its author lists and "cleaned out" unprofitable ones. Like other publishers, HarperCollins has suffered from problems facing the industry such as the financial burden of accepting returns of unsold books from booksellers.
Publishing executives said Monday's announcements could pose new problems for HarperCollins if some agents choose to keep their authors away from the publisher.
"They will have two problems," said one publishing executive who declined to be identified. "Attracting new authors and new material from agents, and keeping the authors they have.

"Perhaps they feel they can't find a buyer, so they have no recourse but to go forward. It's a brave announcement," the executive said. "The question is was it made out of necessity, or a deeply held belief to persevere in the business."
